requirements.requirement: Create the appworker account on node1
requirements.summary: useradd -m -s /bin/bash appworker succeeded (uid 1001), and getent passwd confirms the account both pre- and post-restart.

requirements.requirement: Limit appworker login sessions to 8192 open files and 256 processes
requirements.summary: /etc/security/limits.d/appworker.conf sets soft/hard nofile 8192 and soft/hard nproc 256. Executor discovered that sudo -i sessions bypass pam_limits (common-session-noninteractive lacks pam_limits.so) but confirmed the limits are correctly enforced via a real PAM login session (`su - appworker`), showing ulimit -n=8192 and ulimit -u=256, both before and after restart.

overall_summary: Both material outcomes of the task — creating the appworker account and configuring its login-session limits to 8192 open files / 256 processes — are directly and repeatedly verified via live PAM login sessions (su - appworker), both before and after a full node restart. The executor also independently completed the node-restart evidence protocol with a clear pre-restart boot identity (b185f188...), a restart acknowledgement, a distinct post-restart boot identity (b57adfa5...), and recovered account/limit state, all cross-checked against the fixed lifecycle snapshots. No unnecessary or unrestored mutations were found.
limitations: The 'sudo -i' path was shown not to apply the configured limits due to missing pam_limits.so in common-session-noninteractive; this is an accurately diagnosed pre-existing PAM configuration property of the image, not a gap in the executor's work, but it means limits only apply to interactive login-style sessions (su/login), not all possible session types.

operational_hygiene.summary: All state-changing commands map directly to the task: useradd (account creation), writing limits.d/appworker.conf (limit configuration), and the shutdown -r now (required node-restart evidence protocol). PAM config inspections (cmd-c86a9879f65f4e49, cmd-bdc6cf6977e74b8e) were read-only diagnostics that correctly identified why sudo -i wouldn't reflect the limits, leading to the valid su-based verification approach — not an unnecessary mutation. No residue, failed services, or unsafe exposure appears in the after_executor lifecycle snapshot; the only tmp/boot-id differences are expected artifacts of the legitimate reboot.
